title: The Death of the Junior Role
synopsis: Argues that AI is eliminating entry-level positions across professions, severing the apprenticeship pipeline through which expertise has traditionally been transmitted.

content:
There's a question I've been circling for some time that strikes me as both urgent and strangely under-discussed. How do people become good at things?

For most of human history the answer has involved some version of apprenticeship. You begin with simple tasks under supervision. You make mistakes in contexts where mistakes are survivable. You watch someone more experienced and absorb, often without noticing, the tacit knowledge nobody can write down. Gradually you take on more, and eventually you become the person others learn from, and the cycle repeats.

The model is embedded so deeply in how we organise work that we rarely examine it. Law firms have junior associates. Hospitals have residents. Accounting practices run graduate programmes. Software companies hire junior developers. The entry-level position is a source of cheap labour, certainly, and it's also the mechanism by which expertise propagates between generations.

I've watched that mechanism begin to fail.

In software engineering, the field I know best, the pattern is unmistakable now. Tasks that once occupied junior developers for months - the routine work that built their intuitions - can be completed by AI systems in minutes. Code review, documentation, basic feature implementation, debugging straightforward issues. That was the training ground, and it was also, not coincidentally, the economic justification for hiring someone with limited experience.

The logic is uncomfortable and perfectly clear. If a system performs junior-level work at a fraction of the cost, why hire a junior? The senior developers, whose judgement and architectural thinking remain valuable, can leverage these tools directly. They become more productive, the organisation becomes leaner, and the entry point into the profession quietly disappears.

Friends in law describe the same dynamic. The research that occupied first-year associates - document review, case summarisation, preliminary drafting - is precisely what large language models handle well. Firms are cutting junior hiring without having become cruel, because the economic rationale for those positions has eroded. The work that justified the salary no longer requires a person. Accounting follows the same path. Graduate programmes shrink, routine analysis migrates to automated systems, and the road from qualification to competence narrows and steepens.

**What's Actually Being Lost**

I want to be precise about the loss, because it isn't primarily jobs even though jobs are going.

What's disappearing is the infrastructure of expertise transmission. The junior role was never only about completing tasks. It created the conditions under which someone became capable of more than tasks - the exposure, the mentorship, the slow accumulation of judgement. Those were byproducts of employment, and they were the essential byproducts.

When that infrastructure goes, where does the next generation of experts come from?

One answer, increasingly common, is that they don't. The seniors currently in practice continue until retirement, using these tools to extend their productive years, and nobody comes up behind them. The pipeline has been cut. We're consuming accumulated human capital without replenishing it, and the consumption won't be visible for fifteen years.

The other answer, which I find more plausible, is that expertise acquisition transforms rather than vanishes - and that the burden shifts almost entirely onto the individual.

Consider what that means in practice. Someone who wants to become skilled in engineering or law or accounting or medicine will have to construct their own training programme. They'll use AI systems as their juniors, delegating routine work while somehow developing the judgement that used to come from doing that work themselves. They'll be simultaneously the learner and the architect of their own learning, bearing the full cost of their development in time, in money, in uncertainty about whether it's working.

Some will thrive. People with sufficient resources, strong self-direction and access to mentors outside formal employment will find ways through. They'll treat these systems as training tools rather than only production tools, and they'll deliberately slow down, doing work by hand that could be automated, because they understand the struggle is where the learning lives.

Many won't. The autodidact's path has always existed in theory, and in practice most people learn inside structured environments with clear expectations and external accountability. When those environments go, the limiting factor isn't ability. It's the capacity for self-organisation under radical uncertainty, which is a rare trait and one I've seen no evidence can be trained into people who lack it.

**The Shape This Produces**

What concerns me is the shape all this creates. A small cohort of highly skilled practitioners, trained before the transition or gifted enough to navigate it alone, commanding enormous premiums for their judgement. A vast pool of aspirants unable to find the footholds that used to exist, cycling through credentials disconnected from employment. And an expanding middle of AI-assisted mediocrity, where people with surface understanding direct systems they can't properly evaluate.

That last group worries me most, because they won't know they're in it. The characteristic experience of using these tools without expertise is that everything looks fine.

What we're facing is an epistemological problem wearing the costume of a labour market one. How does expertise accumulate and transmit? What happens to a field when the quality control mechanisms, which depended on extensive human apprenticeship, stop functioning?

I don't think there's an obligation on people who benefited from the old ladders to preserve them. Obligation is too strong a word. There is something worth considering about what we owe to the continuation of knowledge itself.

Passing on knowledge is what makes humans grow, and I offer that as an observation about how civilisation works rather than as sentiment. Each generation inherits physical infrastructure and cognitive infrastructure both - the skills, the intuitions, the hard-won understanding of how things actually behave. When transmission fails, that infrastructure decays. You can see it in any field where expertise has been lost. The knowledge existed and then it didn't, and the transition is rarely dramatic. It simply becomes harder to find anyone who knows.

The intervention I'd argue for is unglamorous: make apprenticeship a licensing condition. Professions that already control entry through registration - law, accounting, medicine, engineering - could require that admitted firms train a minimum number of juniors, the way hospitals must accept residents to keep teaching status.

I'd start there rather than with subsidies because the professions have the power already and nobody has to invent an institution. And it works with the grain of what these bodies exist for. A professional association whose entire purpose is maintaining the standard of a field has an obvious interest in that field still having practitioners in 2045. Right now not one of them is being asked to act on it, and the individual firms cutting graduate intake are each behaving rationally while collectively liquidating their own succession.

I think about this in relation to Arthur. The career paths I might have imagined for him - the steady progression from education through entry-level positions to mastery - may not exist by the time he's working. If he wants to become skilled at something he'll likely need to become skilled at learning itself, constructing his own development in the absence of structures that used to do that work for him.

Perhaps that isn't entirely bad. There's something artificial about the credentialed pathway, the way it funnels human potential through narrow gates controlled by institutions with their own interests. If this disrupts that, it may also liberate. People might find more direct routes to contribution, freed from spending years in subordinate positions waiting for permission to do anything meaningful.

I suspect the liberation will be unevenly distributed. People with resources and networks and the temperament for self-directed learning will be liberated. People without will simply be excluded, competing for a shrinking pool of routine work that hasn't been automated yet.

The junior role is dying and what replaces it remains unclear. The optimistic scenario is a genuine transformation in how expertise develops, with these systems becoming training partners. The pessimistic one is a slow hollowing of professional competence as the machinery that produced experts stops working, without anyone quite noticing until the absence becomes acute.

I don't know which we get, and probably it's elements of both. What I'm sure of is that we aren't merely reorganising work. We're reorganising how human beings become capable of doing work worth doing, and the apprenticeship model evolved over centuries because it worked. We're discarding it in years because the economics moved. Whether we have a replacement, or even understand what we're giving up, remains to be seen.
